title: What is the anatomical position of the appendix?
model_answer:
The [[anat:vermiform appendix]] is a narrow, blind-ended tubular diverticulum arising from the [[anat:posteromedial wall of the caecum]].

- Originates approximately [[pearl:2 cm below the ileocaecal valve]].
- Arises at the [[pearl:convergence of the three taeniae coli]].
- Usually measures approximately [[pearl:6–9 cm]] in adults, although length is variable.
- Has a mesentery called the mesoappendix, containing the [[art:appendicular artery]] and [[vein:veins]].
- The base has a relatively constant position, whereas the tip is highly variable.

:::pearl Surgical importance
the convergence of the taeniae coli helps identify the base during appendicectomy, even when the tip is displaced.
:::

![The caecum and vermiform appendix: the appendix arises where the taeniae coli converge, and the mesoappendix carries its vessels.](/clinical/caecum-appendix-anatomy.jpg)
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why is the anatomical position of the appendix clinically important?
model_answer:
Position determines the location of pain and tenderness, clinical presentation, guarding, rebound tenderness, presence or absence of typical signs, differential diagnosis and surgical difficulty.

- **Retrocecal:** may produce flank or back pain.
- **Pelvic:** may produce suprapubic pain, urinary symptoms or diarrhoea.
- **Subhepatic:** may mimic acute cholecystitis.
- **Left-sided:** may occur with situs inversus or intestinal malrotation.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is McBurney’s point?
model_answer:
The junction of the [[pearl:lateral one-third and medial two-thirds]] of a line joining the [[anat:right anterior superior iliac spine]] (ASIS) to the [[anat:umbilicus]]. It is the classical site of maximal tenderness in acute appendicitis, although tenderness may be displaced according to appendiceal position.

![McBurney’s point, Rovsing’s sign, the psoas sign (retrocaecal appendicitis) and the obturator sign (retrocaecal or pelvic appendicitis).](/clinical/appendicitis-clinical-signs.jpg)
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does the appendix have variable positions?
model_answer: The appendix develops from the caecal diverticulum. As the [[anat:caecum]] descends from the upper abdomen towards the right iliac fossa, rotation, fixation and subsequent growth influence the direction of the appendiceal tip. The base remains relatively constant, but the tip can point in different directions.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the blood supply of the appendix?
model_answer: The [[art:appendicular artery]], usually a branch of the ileocolic artery from the superior mesenteric artery, runs through the mesoappendix. It is essentially an [[art:end artery]] with limited collateral circulation. Severe inflammation and pressure can compromise perfusion, causing [[art:ischaemia]], [[art:gangrene]] and [[warn:perforation]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What are the different anatomical positions of the appendix?
model_answer:
- **Retrocecal:** behind the [[anat:caecum]].
- **Pelvic:** descends into the pelvis.
- **Subcecal:** below the caecum.
- **Preileal:** anterior to the [[anat:terminal ileum]].
- **Postileal:** posterior to the terminal ileum.
- **Paracecal:** alongside the caecum.

Retrocecal and pelvic are commonly encountered. Exact distributions vary between anatomical studies and populations.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Which is the most common position?
model_answer: [[pearl:Retrocecal is commonly reported as the most frequent position]], although exact distribution varies between anatomical studies and populations.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Which position is associated with atypical clinical presentation?
model_answer:
- **Retrocecal:** flank or back pain.
- **Pelvic:** suprapubic pain, urinary symptoms and diarrhoea.
- **Subhepatic:** right upper quadrant pain.
- **Preileal/postileal:** variable pain and sometimes atypical tenderness.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Which position is associated with psoas irritation?
model_answer: Retrocecal appendix. The inflamed appendix lies close to the [[anat:psoas muscle]] and may irritate it, producing a positive [[pearl:psoas sign]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Which position is associated with obturator irritation?
model_answer: Pelvic appendix. The inflamed appendix may lie close to the [[anat:obturator internus]] muscle and produce a positive [[pearl:obturator sign]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What are the clinical differences between pelvic and retrocecal appendicitis?
model_answer:
**Pelvic appendix:**

- **Position:** descends into pelvis.
- **Pain:** suprapubic or lower abdominal.
- RIF tenderness may be minimal.
- Urinary symptoms (dysuria, frequency) and bowel symptoms (diarrhoea, tenesmus) may occur.
- [[pearl:Obturator sign]] may be positive.
- Rectal or vaginal tenderness may be present in selected patients.

**Retrocecal appendix:**

- **Position:** behind [[anat:caecum]].
- **Pain:** right flank, back or RIF.
- Anterior RIF tenderness may be less obvious.
- [[pearl:Psoas sign]] may be positive.
- Urinary and bowel symptoms are less typical.

These are tendencies, not absolute rules.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does pelvic appendicitis cause diarrhoea?
model_answer: The inflamed appendix may irritate the [[anat:rectum]] and adjacent pelvic bowel, causing increased rectal activity and frequent bowel movements.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does pelvic appendicitis cause urinary symptoms?
model_answer: The appendix may lie close to the [[anat:urinary bladder]] or [[anat:right ureter]], causing dysuria, frequency, urgency and occasionally microscopic haematuria.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why might abdominal examination be relatively normal in pelvic appendicitis?
model_answer: The appendix is deep in the pelvis and away from the [[anat:anterior abdominal wall]]. There may be minimal RIF tenderness or guarding. Rectal or pelvic examination may reveal tenderness in selected patients.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does retrocecal appendicitis produce back or flank pain?
model_answer: The appendix lies posterior to the [[anat:caecum]], close to the [[anat:posterior abdominal wall]] and [[anat:psoas muscle]]. Inflammation can irritate these structures and produce right flank or back pain.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why can RIF tenderness be absent?
model_answer: The [[anat:caecum]] lies anterior to the appendix and may partially shield it from the [[anat:anterior abdominal wall]], so inflammation may be more pronounced posteriorly.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why is the psoas sign positive?
model_answer: The inflamed retrocecal appendix irritates the adjacent [[anat:psoas muscle]]. Stretching or contracting the muscle reproduces pain.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: How do you elicit the psoas sign?
model_answer:
**Two methods:**

1. Place the patient on the left side and passively extend the right hip.
2. With the patient supine, ask them to flex the right hip against resistance.

A positive test produces pain in the right lower abdomen.

![McBurney’s point, Rovsing’s sign, the psoas sign (retrocaecal appendicitis) and the obturator sign (retrocaecal or pelvic appendicitis).](/clinical/appendicitis-clinical-signs.jpg)
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: How do you elicit the obturator sign?
model_answer: With the patient supine, flex the right hip and knee to approximately 90 degrees, then internally rotate the hip by moving the right ankle laterally. Hypogastric or right lower abdominal pain suggests [[anat:obturator internus]] irritation, as may occur with a pelvic appendix.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the classical sequence of pain in acute appendicitis?
model_answer:
1. [[nerve:Visceral pain]] around the [[anat:umbilicus]].
2. Migration of pain to the right iliac fossa.
3. Localised [[nerve:somatic pain]] with tenderness and guarding as adjacent [[anat:parietal peritoneum]] becomes inflamed.

![Pain in acute appendicitis: vague periumbilical pain first, then sharp pain localised to McBurney’s point in the right iliac fossa. Inset: the variable positions of the appendix.](/clinical/appendicitis-pain-pathway.jpg)
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does pain initially occur around the umbilicus?
model_answer: Early inflammation stimulates [[nerve:visceral afferent nerve fibres]]. These travel with [[nerve:sympathetic pathways]] to approximately the [[nerve:T10 spinal cord segment]]. Visceral pain is poorly localised and is perceived around the umbilicus.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does pain later migrate to the right iliac fossa?
model_answer: Progressive inflammation involves the [[anat:parietal peritoneum]] adjacent to the appendix. [[nerve:Somatic innervation]] produces well-localised pain, so the pain is perceived in the RIF.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What are the different types of pain involved in appendicitis?
model_answer:
- **Visceral:** stimulation of [[nerve:visceral afferents]]; dull, poorly localised and commonly periumbilical.
- **Somatic:** irritation of [[anat:parietal peritoneum]]; sharp, well-localised RIF pain.
- **Referred:** pain perceived away from the diseased organ due to convergence of visceral and somatic [[nerve:sensory pathways]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the difference between visceral and somatic pain?
model_answer:
**Visceral pain:** poorly localised, dull or cramping, often midline, associated with early appendiceal inflammation.

**Somatic pain:** well localised, sharp, aggravated by movement/coughing/percussion, associated with parietal peritoneal inflammation.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does coughing or walking aggravate pain in appendicitis?
model_answer: Movement displaces and stretches the inflamed [[anat:parietal peritoneum]], producing pain, particularly when localised [[warn:peritonitis]] is present.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Does every patient develop classical pain migration?
model_answer: No. Atypical presentations are more common in children, elderly patients, pregnant women and patients with unusual appendiceal positions. Absence of classical migration [[warn:does not exclude appendicitis]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the difference between obstructive and non-obstructive appendicitis?
model_answer:
**Obstructive appendicitis:** mechanical blockage of the lumen. Causes include appendicolith/fecalith, [[anat:lymphoid hyperplasia]], parasites (particularly Enterobius vermicularis), foreign bodies (rare), appendiceal tumours, fibrosis or strictures. Obstruction prevents drainage and can increase intraluminal pressure.

**Non-obstructive appendicitis:** inflammation develops without demonstrable mechanical obstruction. Possible mechanisms include primary mucosal inflammation, enteric microorganisms, infection-associated inflammation and altered mucosal immune responses. Exact pathogenesis is not fully established.

Obstruction is a classical mechanism, not an absolute requirement.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Explain the pathophysiology of acute obstructive appendicitis.
model_answer:
1. Luminal obstruction by a faecolith, [[anat:lymphoid hyperplasia]], parasite, foreign body or neoplasm.
2. Continued [[anat:mucus secretion]] despite obstruction.
3. Accumulation of secretions and gas increases intraluminal pressure and distends the appendix.
4. Low-pressure [[vein:venous and lymphatic]] vessels are compressed, causing [[vein:congestion]], impaired drainage and wall oedema.
5. Progressive pressure may compromise [[art:arterial perfusion]], causing [[art:ischaemia]].
6. Bacteria proliferate and invade damaged mucosa; common organisms include Escherichia coli, Bacteroides fragilis and other enteric Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms.
7. Severe ischaemia and inflammation cause [[art:gangrene]].
8. Necrotic wall may perforate, causing local abscess, phlegmon, generalised peritonitis or sepsis.

:::remember Sequence
obstruction → mucus accumulation → raised pressure → venous/lymphatic obstruction → oedema/congestion → arterial compromise/ischaemia → bacterial invasion/inflammation → gangrene → perforation.
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why is the appendicular artery clinically important?
model_answer: It is essentially an [[art:end artery]] with limited collateral circulation. Severe inflammation and raised intraluminal pressure can compromise its blood supply, predisposing to [[art:gangrene]] and [[warn:perforation]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is an appendicolith?
model_answer:
A calcified or inspissated mass of faecal material within the appendiceal lumen. It may cause obstruction and is associated with increased risk of [[warn:complicated appendicitis]] and [[warn:failure of antibiotic-only treatment]].

![CT of the appendix: a normal appendix (≤ 6 mm) compared with appendicitis showing dilatation with fluid (> 6 mm), periappendiceal inflammation and an appendicolith.](/clinical/ct-appendicitis-findings.jpg)
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the difference between an appendicular mass and an appendicular abscess?
model_answer:
**Appendicular mass (phlegmon):** inflammatory mass formed by the appendix, adjacent bowel loops, omentum and surrounding tissues; it may not contain drainable pus.

**Appendicular abscess:** a localised collection of pus resulting from [[warn:perforated]] appendicitis.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What are the differential diagnoses of RIF pain?
model_answer:
**Gastrointestinal:** acute appendicitis, mesenteric lymphadenitis, Meckel’s diverticulitis, Crohn’s disease/terminal ileitis, infectious ileitis, caecal diverticulitis, right-sided colitis, gastroenteritis, intestinal obstruction, intussusception, caecal carcinoma, [[warn:perforated]] bowel, constipation.

**Urological:** right ureteric stone/renal colic, acute pyelonephritis, UTI, cystitis, urinary retention.

**Gynaecological:** [[warn:ectopic pregnancy]], [[warn:ovarian torsion]], ruptured ovarian cyst, haemorrhagic corpus luteum, PID, salpingitis, tubo-ovarian [[warn:abscess]], endometriosis, mittelschmerz, dysmenorrhoea.

**Other:** right lower lobe pneumonia, abdominal wall strain, psoas abscess, hernia, [[warn:testicular torsion]] ([[nerve:referred pain]]), diabetic ketoacidosis.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: How can clinical presentation guide the RIF pain differential?
model_answer:
- **Migratory periumbilical → RIF pain:** appendicitis.
- **Colicky pain radiating to groin:** ureteric stone.
- **RIF pain with diarrhoea:** gastroenteritis, ileitis or pelvic appendicitis.
- **RIF pain with vaginal bleeding:** [[warn:ectopic pregnancy]] must be considered.
- **Sudden unilateral pelvic pain:** [[warn:ovarian torsion]] or ruptured cyst.
- **RIF pain with urinary frequency:** UTI or pelvic appendicitis.
- **Pain after recent viral illness:** mesenteric lymphadenitis.
- **Chronic diarrhoea and weight loss:** Crohn’s disease.
- **Fever with cervical motion tenderness:** PID.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is mesenteric lymphadenitis?
model_answer: Inflammation and enlargement of [[anat:mesenteric lymph nodes]], usually associated with infection. It commonly affects children and young adults and can mimic acute appendicitis.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is Meckel’s diverticulum?
model_answer: A congenital true diverticulum caused by persistence of the [[anat:vitelline]] (omphalomesenteric) duct. Usually lies on the antimesenteric border of the ileum. Complications include diverticulitis, GI [[art:bleeding]], intestinal obstruction, intussusception and [[warn:perforation]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What investigations would you request in a female patient with RIF pain?
model_answer:
- [[pearl:Pregnancy test]] (urine or serum β-hCG).
- CBC and CRP.
- Urinalysis.
- Renal function and electrolytes.
- Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound.
- CT abdomen/pelvis when indicated.
- MRI when appropriate, particularly in pregnancy after inconclusive ultrasound.

Always exclude [[warn:ectopic pregnancy]] in a patient of reproductive potential.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is appendiceal diverticulosis?
model_answer: Presence of one or more diverticula arising from the wall of the [[anat:vermiform appendix]]. It is uncommon and may be found incidentally during appendicectomy or on histopathology.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What are the types of appendiceal diverticula?
model_answer:
**Congenital/true diverticulum:** rare; contains all layers of the appendiceal wall; usually developmental.

**Acquired/false diverticulum:** more common; mucosa and submucosa herniate through the muscular wall; may be associated with raised intraluminal pressure or wall abnormalities.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is appendiceal diverticulitis?
model_answer: Inflammation of one or more appendiceal diverticula. It can resemble acute appendicitis but is associated in published series with a higher risk of [[warn:perforation]] and complications.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the difference between appendicitis and appendiceal diverticulitis?
model_answer: Appendicitis affects the appendix itself and is common. Appendiceal diverticulitis affects an appendiceal diverticulum and is rare. Both can present similarly with RIF pain and fever. Diverticulitis has a higher reported [[warn:perforation]] rate; diagnosis may be made by imaging or histopathology. Appendicectomy is generally recommended for symptomatic disease.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the treatment of appendiceal diverticulitis?
model_answer: Appendicectomy is generally recommended for symptomatic appendiceal diverticulitis because of [[warn:perforation]] risk and reported association with [[warn:appendiceal neoplasms]]. Histopathological examination is important.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the clinical importance of appendiceal diverticulosis?
model_answer: It may cause recurrent RIF pain or acute diverticulitis, has a higher reported [[warn:perforation]] rate than ordinary appendicitis, may be associated with [[warn:appendiceal neoplasms]] in some series, and can be difficult to diagnose preoperatively.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: How do you differentiate acute appendicitis from a ruptured ovarian cyst?
model_answer:
**Appendicitis:** often gradual onset; classically periumbilical pain migrating to RIF; anorexia, nausea/vomiting and low-grade fever may occur; no specific menstrual relationship; vaginal [[art:bleeding]] is not typical.

**Ruptured ovarian cyst:** often sudden unilateral lower abdominal/pelvic pain; may relate to ovulation or luteal phase; vaginal spotting may occur; adnexal tenderness and ultrasound evidence of cyst/free pelvic fluid may be present. Fever is usually absent unless another complication exists.

There is substantial clinical overlap; pregnancy testing and imaging are important.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is a ruptured ovarian cyst?
model_answer: [[warn:Rupture]] of a fluid-filled ovarian cyst, releasing its contents into the peritoneal cavity and causing sudden pelvic pain. Examples include functional follicular cyst, corpus luteum cyst and [[art:haemorrhagic]] ovarian cyst.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does a ruptured ovarian cyst cause sudden pain?
model_answer: [[warn:Rupture]] releases cyst contents into the peritoneal cavity, irritating pelvic peritoneum. With a [[art:haemorrhagic]] cyst, blood may accumulate in the pelvis and cause additional peritoneal irritation.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What clues suggest a ruptured ovarian cyst rather than appendicitis?
model_answer: Sudden unilateral pelvic pain, association with ovulation or menstrual cycle, possible vaginal spotting, adnexal tenderness and ultrasound showing an ovarian cyst/free pelvic fluid. Typical migratory pain is usually absent. Clinical overlap remains substantial.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the most important diagnosis to exclude in a reproductive-age woman with sudden pelvic pain?
model_answer: [[warn:Ectopic pregnancy]]. [[pearl:Always perform a pregnancy test]], even if the patient reports normal menstruation or uses contraception.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: How do you investigate suspected appendicitis versus ruptured ovarian cyst?
model_answer: [[pearl:Pregnancy test]] (β-hCG), CBC, CRP, urinalysis, abdominal/pelvic ultrasound and transvaginal ultrasound when appropriate. CT may be used if appendicitis remains suspected and the patient is not pregnant. MRI is useful in selected situations, including pregnancy when ultrasound is inconclusive.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the treatment of a ruptured ovarian cyst?
model_answer:
**Depends on severity:**

- Stable patient with uncomplicated [[warn:rupture]]: conservative management, analgesia and observation.
- **Significant haemorrhage:** resuscitation and urgent gynaecological assessment.
- [[art:Haemodynamic instability]] or [[art:ongoing bleeding]]: operative intervention may be required, preserving the ovary whenever possible.

A [[art:haemorrhagic]] rupture can be [[warn:life-threatening]]; not every case is suitable for conservative management.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is intestinal obstruction?
model_answer:
Partial or complete interruption of the normal passage of intestinal contents through the GI tract. It may affect small or large bowel.

**Mechanical:** physical blockage of the lumen.

**Functional:** failure of normal intestinal motility without a physical blockage, as in paralytic ileus.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What are the types of intestinal obstruction?
model_answer:
**By mechanism:** mechanical or functional.

**By degree:** partial or complete.

**By blood supply:** simple (no [[art:blood supply]] compromise) or [[art:strangulated]] ([[art:vascular compromise]]).

**By site:** small bowel obstruction (SBO) or large bowel obstruction (LBO).

**By configuration:** open-loop or [[warn:closed-loop]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is closed-loop obstruction?
model_answer:
A segment of bowel is obstructed at two points, preventing proximal and distal decompression. It causes rapid distension and increases risk of [[art:strangulation]], [[art:ischaemia]], necrosis and [[warn:perforation]]. Examples include volvulus, an incarcerated loop in certain hernias and an adhesive band obstructing at two points.

![CT showing the whirl sign of a volvulus: the mesentery twisted around its vessels (arrows), with dilated gas-filled bowel.](/clinical/volvulus-whirl-sign-ct.jpg)
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is strangulated intestinal obstruction?
model_answer: Obstruction associated with [[art:impairment of blood supply]] to the affected bowel. Progression: [[vein:venous obstruction]] → congestion → bowel wall oedema → arterial compromise → [[art:ischaemia]] → [[art:gangrene]] → perforation → [[warn:peritonitis]] and sepsis. It is a [[warn:surgical emergency]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Explain the pathophysiology of intestinal obstruction.
model_answer:
1. Mechanical blockage prevents normal passage of intestinal contents (e.g. adhesions, hernia, tumour, volvulus, intussusception).
2. Swallowed air, GI secretions, food/fluids and biliary/pancreatic secretions accumulate proximal to the obstruction.
3. Proximal bowel dilates; distal bowel becomes relatively collapsed.
4. Initially, [[anat:peristalsis]] increases to overcome the blockage, producing colicky pain and high-pitched/tinkling sounds. Later motility may decrease due to fatigue, [[art:ischaemia]] and inflammation.
5. Rising intraluminal pressure impairs [[vein:venous and lymphatic]] drainage and eventually [[art:arterial supply]].
6. Fluid accumulates in bowel lumen and wall (third-spacing); vomiting and reduced absorption add losses, causing [[warn:dehydration]], hypovolaemia, [[warn:electrolyte disturbance]] and [[warn:AKI]].
7. Repeated vomiting can cause loss of HCl, hypochloraemia, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, especially in proximal SBO. Advanced ischaemia or sepsis causes lactic acidosis.
8. Stasis promotes bacterial overgrowth; bacteria/toxins may cross damaged bowel wall, causing systemic inflammation and sepsis.
9. In strangulation, vascular compromise causes ischaemia, necrosis and possible perforation, leading to peritonitis, sepsis and multi-organ dysfunction.

:::remember Sequence
obstruction → fluid/gas accumulation → proximal distension → raised pressure → venous congestion/oedema → sequestration/dehydration → arterial compromise/ischaemia → necrosis/perforation → peritonitis/sepsis.
:::

![How obstruction progresses: distension and colicky pain, vomiting and third-space fluid loss, then ischaemia, necrosis and peritonitis.](/clinical/obstruction-pathophysiology.jpg)
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does intestinal obstruction cause dehydration?
model_answer: Fluid accumulates within the bowel lumen and wall; vomiting and reduced absorption cause additional fluid loss.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does intestinal obstruction cause metabolic alkalosis?
model_answer: Repeated vomiting causes loss of [[anat:gastric hydrochloric acid]]: hydrogen and chloride ions are lost, increasing bicarbonate relative to hydrogen ions. [[warn:Volume depletion]] and [[warn:potassium depletion]] help maintain the alkalosis.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does intestinal obstruction cause metabolic acidosis in advanced cases?
model_answer: Bowel [[art:ischaemia]] and systemic hypoperfusion cause anaerobic metabolism and accumulation of [[art:lactic acid]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does the abdomen become distended?
model_answer: Gas and fluid accumulate in dilated bowel proximal to the obstruction.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does the patient initially experience colicky pain?
model_answer: Intestinal [[anat:smooth muscle]] contracts forcefully against the obstruction, producing intermittent waves of pain.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why does colicky pain become continuous in strangulation?
model_answer: [[art:Vascular compromise]], [[art:ischaemia]] and inflammation stimulate persistent pain pathways. Continuous severe pain is a [[warn:warning sign]] of possible strangulation.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What are the most common causes of intestinal obstruction?
model_answer: **Classical major causes:** adhesions, hernias and [[warn:malignancy]]. Relative frequency depends on small versus large bowel and geography.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What are the causes of small bowel obstruction?
model_answer:
- **Adhesions:** fibrous bands kink or compress bowel.
- **Hernias:** bowel trapped in a hernia defect.
- **Tumours:** intraluminal or extrinsic compression.
- **Volvulus:** bowel twists around its [[anat:mesentery]].
- **Intussusception:** one bowel segment telescopes into another.
- **Crohn’s disease:** inflammatory strictures.
- **Gallstone ileus:** gallstone enters bowel through a biliary-enteric fistula.
- **Bezoar:** accumulated indigestible material.
- **Radiation enteritis:** fibrotic strictures.

Adhesions are the [[pearl:most common cause]] of SBO in patients with previous abdominal surgery.

![Four mechanical causes of bowel obstruction: adhesions, herniation, volvulus and intussusception.](/clinical/bowel-obstruction-causes.jpg)
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What are the causes of large bowel obstruction?
model_answer:
- **Colorectal carcinoma:** narrows the lumen.
- Sigmoid volvulus or caecal volvulus.
- **Diverticular stricture:** fibrosis following diverticulitis.
- Faecal impaction.
- Inflammatory strictures, including inflammatory bowel disease.

Colorectal cancer is the [[pearl:most common cause]] in many high-income settings; distribution varies geographically.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: How can causes be classified by the site of pathology?
model_answer:
**Intraluminal:** gallstone, bezoar, foreign body, faecal impaction.

**Intramural:** tumour, inflammatory stricture, congenital stenosis.

**Extramural:** adhesions, hernias, volvulus, external compression.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the difference between small and large bowel obstruction?
model_answer:
**SBO:** vomiting usually early; distension variable and may be less marked; central colicky pain; adhesions common, especially after surgery.

**LBO:** vomiting usually late; distension often marked; lower abdominal colicky pain; [[warn:malignancy]] is a major cause in adults in many populations.

Constipation/[[warn:obstipation]] can occur in both. These are typical patterns, not absolute diagnostic rules.

![Erect abdominal X-ray in small bowel obstruction: dilated small-bowel loops with multiple air–fluid levels (arrows).](/clinical/sbo-erect-air-fluid-levels.jpg)
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is obstipation?
model_answer: Complete inability to pass both stool and flatus. It is an important feature of complete obstruction, although stool or flatus distal to the obstruction may still be passed initially.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What are intestinal adhesions?
model_answer: Abnormal fibrous bands of scar tissue connecting surfaces of organs or tissues that are normally separate. In the abdomen they may connect bowel loops, bowel to abdominal wall, bowel to omentum or bowel to pelvic organs. They are an important cause of postoperative SBO.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What causes adhesions?
model_answer: **Most important cause:** previous abdominal or pelvic surgery. Other causes include [[warn:peritonitis]], intra-abdominal infection, appendicitis, diverticulitis, tuberculosis, endometriosis, radiation therapy and abdominal trauma.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Explain the pathophysiology of adhesion formation.
model_answer:
1. Peritoneal injury: surgery, infection or inflammation damages mesothelium.
2. Inflammatory response: inflammatory mediators and coagulation pathways activate.
3. Fibrin deposition occurs on injured surfaces.
4. If [[anat:fibrinolysis]] is inadequate, fibrin persists and bridges adjacent surfaces.
5. Fibroblasts migrate into the fibrin matrix.
6. Collagen is deposited, converting the temporary fibrin bridge into a permanent fibrous adhesion.

:::remember Sequence
injury → inflammation → fibrin deposition → reduced fibrinolysis → fibroblast proliferation → collagen deposition → permanent adhesion.
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: How do adhesions cause intestinal obstruction?
model_answer: An adhesive band can compress bowel externally, kink or angulate a loop, trap bowel beneath a band, create two points of obstruction ([[warn:closed loop]]), or constrict the [[anat:mesentery]] and compromise [[art:blood supply]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why is adhesive intestinal obstruction common after appendicectomy?
model_answer: Surgery in the RIF can cause peritoneal and adjacent bowel inflammation or injury. Healing may produce fibrous adhesions, particularly after [[warn:complicated appendicitis]], [[warn:perforation]] or [[warn:peritonitis]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the treatment of adhesive small bowel obstruction?
model_answer:
Non-operative management is appropriate when there is no [[warn:peritonitis]], [[art:strangulation]], bowel ischaemia or [[warn:perforation]]:

- Nil per os (NPO).
- Nasogastric decompression.
- IV fluid replacement and electrolyte correction.
- Urinary catheter and urine-output monitoring when indicated.
- Serial abdominal examination.
- CBC, renal function, electrolytes and lactate.
- CT assessment and water-soluble contrast challenge when appropriate.

Bologna guidelines report non-operative treatment is effective in approximately [[pearl:70–90%]] of adhesive SBO cases.

Surgery is indicated for peritonitis, suspected strangulation, identified [[art:ischaemia]], perforation or [[warn:failure of conservative management]]. Operation is usually adhesiolysis; resect bowel if nonviable.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is adhesiolysis?
model_answer: Surgical division or release of fibrous adhesions to relieve obstruction. It may be laparoscopic in selected patients or performed through open laparotomy.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: How can postoperative adhesions be prevented?
model_answer: Gentle tissue handling, minimising tissue trauma, meticulous haemostasis, preventing infection, minimising foreign-body contamination, minimally invasive surgery when appropriate and adhesion barriers in selected cases.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why do we insert a nasogastric tube in intestinal obstruction?
model_answer:
To decompress the stomach and proximal GI tract: remove accumulated gastric/intestinal secretions, reduce vomiting and distension, reduce [[warn:aspiration risk]], relieve discomfort, quantify ongoing fluid losses and assist conservative management.

![Chest X-ray checking a nasogastric tube: it runs down the midline, bisects the carina, crosses the diaphragm at the gastro-oesophageal junction and its tip lies in the stomach.](/clinical/ng-tube-position-cxr.jpg)
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What are the contents of NG aspirate in intestinal obstruction?
model_answer:
**The pattern depends on level and duration:**

- Gastric outlet/very proximal obstruction: gastric fluid, often food particles.
- **Proximal SBO:** gastric and bilious fluid.
- **Distal SBO:** often bilious or enteric fluid; may become [[warn:faeculent]] in advanced cases.
- **LBO:** vomiting tends to occur late and may become faeculent when severe or prolonged.

These are typical patterns, not reliable diagnostic rules; volume and content are influenced by duration, [[anat:ileocaecal valve]] competence, reflux and previous vomiting.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why is the aspirate bilious in small bowel obstruction?
model_answer: Intestinal contents containing bile may reflux proximally into the stomach when bowel becomes obstructed and distended. Bile enters the [[anat:duodenum]] through the [[anat:ampulla of Vater]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: Why can vomiting become faeculent in advanced intestinal obstruction?
model_answer: Prolonged obstruction causes intestinal stasis, bacterial proliferation and accumulation of intestinal contents. Reflux of stagnant contents proximally can produce foul-smelling, [[warn:faeculent]] vomitus.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What does a large volume of NG aspirate indicate?
model_answer: It may indicate significant fluid accumulation in the stomach and proximal bowel, and substantial ongoing fluid/electrolyte losses that need measurement and replacement.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What electrolyte abnormalities can occur with prolonged NG drainage?
model_answer: [[warn:Hypokalaemia]], [[warn:hypochloraemia]], [[warn:metabolic alkalosis]] and volume depletion. Measure losses and replace according to fluid status and laboratory results.
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook

title: What is the significance of faeculent NG aspirate?
model_answer: It suggests severe or prolonged intestinal obstruction with significant stasis and reflux. It warrants urgent reassessment but does not independently prove [[art:strangulation]] or [[warn:perforation]].
source: Dr. Salah — Appendix & Intestinal Obstruction workbook
